text: The front from Kharkiv to Kherson is mostly open steppe and forest-steppe farmland on chernozem (chornozem, "black earth").
notes: The sentence itself is uncited; it cites the sources the block gives for the landscape description.

text: Large fields on the front are separated by planted windbreak belts, called lisosmuhy in Ukrainian (sing. lisosmuha) and lesopolosy in Russian.
Natural woodland in the eastern and southern Ukrainian steppe is scarce and occurs mainly along river banks and in gullies (balkas).

cites.quote: mainly along rivers banks and in gullies

text: The exceptions to scarce natural woodland are the sandy pine forests on the left-bank terraces of the Siverskyi Donets, at Lyman, Kreminna and Serebrianka.
The Donbas has mining towns with terrikons (coal spoil heaps) from 40 m to over 100 m high.
The Donbas landscape includes coke and chemical plants and Soviet apartment blocks alongside its mining towns.
On the steppe front the treeline is the basic tactical unit: it provides cover, a firing position, an infiltration corridor and an artillery target.
The tactical value of a treeline swings with the seasons: foliage in summer, bare branches and snow in winter, and mud (rasputitsa, Ukrainian bezdorizhzhia) in spring and autumn.
In e8–e9, drone saturation has widened the contested zone from about 1 km to several km.
In e8–e9, survival at the front depends on concealment more than on firepower because of drone saturation.

For procedural generation, the front-line landscape is regular: a rectilinear Soviet-era field and belt grid laid over a dendritic network of gullies and river valleys, with villages strung along the valleys.
notes: Uncited synthesis in the overview; cites the §2.7 measurement sources.

text: Measured in five 10 × 10 km front-line sample boxes, belt-bounded blocks are typically about 0.5–0.6 km × 1.0–1.3 km, with a median field area of 40–65 ha.
In the five front-line sample boxes, small villages are linear strips a few hundred metres wide.
Several open datasets can calibrate procedural terrain generation for the front: OSM, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover, Sentinel-2 and Dynamic World.
Ukrainian shelterbelts date from 1809, when Vasyl Lomykovsky planted trees around fields in Poltava gubernia.
Shelterbelts in Ukraine were studied by Dokuchaev and Vysotsky in the 1890s.
Shelterbelts in Ukraine were planted systematically in 1938–39 and 1948–52.
The 1948 "Great Stalin Plan for the Transformation of Nature" drove the largest wave of shelterbelt planting in Ukraine.

mentions.name: Great Stalin Plan for the Transformation of Nature

text: By a Ukrainian NGO's count, 440,000 ha of field-protective belts were planted in Ukraine in the ten years from 1950.
By a Ukrainian NGO's count, another 154,500 ha of field-protective belts were planted in Ukraine in the 20 years from 1971.
Ukraine had about 400,000 ha of shelterbelts in the early 1990s.
After the collective farms were dissolved, many Ukrainian shelterbelts ended up with unclear ownership and outside the land cadastre, and they degraded.
The Ukrainian government's 2020 rules and the national Technology Needs Assessment target reconstruction of about 85,000 ha of shelterbelts by 2030.
The front-line shelterbelts in e1–e9 are mostly 50–75-year-old Soviet plantings, often gappy or fragmented.
Hlib Parfonov writes that front-line shelterbelts are typically three to four rows of trees deep.

cites.quote: typically three to four rows of trees deep

text: Hlib Parfonov writes that front-line shelterbelts are rarely more than twenty to thirty metres wide.

text: Hlib Parfonov writes that front-line shelterbelts have 10–30 m gaps left for farm machinery.
Shelterbelts mapped as narrow wood strips in OSM have a median canopy width of 20–27 m across the five sample boxes.

text: Canopy width overstates the planted width of a shelterbelt: Ukrainian foresters convert remote-sensed canopy width to stem-to-stem width with a factor of 0.46.
A studied Left-Bank forest-steppe oak windbreak is 15 m wide, planted as oak "nests" at 5 × 3 m with 5 m alleys and companion and shrub rows.
A Luhansk soil-erosion study found about 10 m to be the optimal shelterbelt width for trapping blown soil.
Mature shelterbelts reach 19.6–23.4 m in height.
Hlib Parfonov describes the front-line belt grid as dense, at intervals of 300 to 400 m longitudinally and 1,000 to 2,000 m laterally.

cites.quote: intervals of 300 to 400 meters longitudinally and 1,000 to 2,000 meters laterally

text: OSM and Sentinel-2 measurements put the main belts somewhat further apart than Parfonov's 300–400 m: at Huliaipole the median main-belt spacing is 549 m (p10–p90 379–990 m) and cross-belts are about 1.1–1.3 km apart.
At Robotyne the measured spacing is about 0.5–0.6 km between main belts and 1.0–1.2 km between cross-belts.
In the Oleshky district of Kherson oblast the distance between shelterbelts is 350–780 m, averaging 550 m.

text: With shelterbelts about 20 m tall, main belts on the front stand roughly 25–30 tree heights apart.
notes: The file marks this as derived; Soviet design norms stated as multiples of tree height were not found.

text: Kherson oblast alone had about 30,000 km of windbreaks, roughly 1 km per km² of oblast.
A full two-way shelterbelt grid at the measured spacings implies about 2.5–3 km of belt per km² of cropland.

text: The best-mapped OSM sample boxes reach a mapped shelterbelt density of 1.35 km/km².
In Luhansk oblast the main harmful (deflation) winds come from the east.
Main shelterbelts are laid across the prevailing wind, so in Luhansk oblast they tend to run roughly north–south.
The measured belt grids are near-cardinal at Huliaipole (N–S main belts, E–W cross-belts) and at Robotyne (roughly E–W and N–S, 10° off).
The measured belt grids are oblique (WNW–ESE and NNE–SSW) east of Kupiansk and irregular in the dissected ground south of Chasiv Yar.
In Ukrainian shelterbelts, oak, pine, birch and poplar form the tall layer, with linden, maple, apple and pear lower down.
Oak-led shelterbelts with companion trees and a shrub understorey are common.
Treelines hold forward trenches, while reserves, artillery and logistics sit 8–15 km back in treelines, woods and towns.

text: The Ukrainian soldier-analyst Hlib Parfonov bases his 2026 treeline report on Russian tactical guidance and his own front-line service.

Parfonov finds the longitudinal attack, in which troops enter a belt from its flank and fight along its interior, to be the predominant treeline assault method, employed by both Russian and Ukrainian forces.

cites.quote: the predominant method in current practice, employed by both Russian and Ukrainian forces

text: Parfonov judges the perpendicular attack across the open field into a belt to be operationally unviable in the majority of cases because of mines, anti-tank weapons, artillery and exposure.

cites.quote: operationally unviable in the majority of cases

Belt intersections are avoided as command-post sites because they are obvious aiming points.
In spring 2026 Russian forces tried to use new foliage to move infantry along treelines on foot, on motorcycles or on quad bikes.
Near Pokrovsk in winter 2024–25, an exposed 80 × 30 m trench cut into the 1 km-long CHAI treeline was destroyed.

text: Near Pokrovsk in winter 2024–25, two concealed fighting holes in the undergrowth of the CHAI treeline held for 10 days.
In summer 2023 leaves protected treeline positions from drones and precision fires; autumn leaf-fall and then snow exposed them.
Parfonov writes that summer canopy substantially degrades FPV effectiveness.
Parfonov writes that foliage conceals both sides from late spring to early autumn, and bare branches expose both from late autumn to early spring.
Sustained barrages reduced some treelines to "piles of split wood and tree branches".

Large fields dominate post-Soviet countries, per a search summary of the global field-size study.

text: Ukraine has more than 5 million fields of at least 1 ha (2021–2023).
Fields near the front are often abandoned and hard to delineate.
In the game, abandoned fields near the front should become weedy fallow.
Nationally, cultivated area in Ukraine fell by 2.5 Mha (−8.5%) from 2021 to 2024.
By 2024, 7% of Ukraine's cropland (about 2.2 Mha) was abandoned.
Of Ukraine's abandoned cropland, 1.1–1.7 Mha, primarily along the front lines, may be permanently lost.
Up to 0.47 Mha of Ukrainian cropland was recultivated in 2024 alone, far more than official demining covers.
Open fields are kill zones watched by drones; movement happens along or through the belts, and crossing a field between belts is the dangerous phase.
Paved roads become the only routes for heavy vehicles in mud season.
Primary to tertiary roads run at 0.13–0.22 km per km² in the five sample boxes.
Mapped highway=track density is 0.3–0.9 km/km² in the sample boxes where tracks are mapped at all; Huliaipole E has almost none in OSM.
Only 4–24% of mapped track length in the sample boxes lies within 40 m of a mapped belt, so "a track along every belt" is not supported by OSM.

text: Satellite imagery of the sample boxes shows tracks along some belt edges and across fields, which OSM maps incompletely.
Balkas and yary (gullies and ravines) cut the steppe interfluves and host most of the natural woodland.
Balkas and yary dissect the high right bank of the Siverskyi Donets.
In the Sentinel-2 sample mosaics, wooded balkas show up as dendritic strips several kilometres long that cut diagonally across the belt grid.
In the Sentinel-2 sample mosaics, villages sit along wooded balkas or at their heads (west of Pokrovsk, east of Kupiansk, east of Huliaipole).
Ravines are mapped as their own class of protective plantation.
Tactically, a gully separates one "elevated platform" (a flat interfluve) from the next.
At Rivnopil in June 2023, Russian positions were vulnerable because a gully cut them off from the next platform they held.
Assault troops use "folds in the ground" to approach a shelterbelt.
For the game, balkas are covered approach routes, natural anti-vehicle obstacles and boundaries between defensible platforms.
The right bank of the Siverskyi Donets is usually high, sometimes with chalk cliffs (the Sviatohirsk / Holy Mountains area).

cites.quote: usually high, sometimes with chalk cliffs

text: The left bank of the Siverskyi Donets is low, with swamps, lakes and oxbows.
The bank asymmetry of the Siverskyi Donets means the high right bank dominates and the low left bank floods.
The forests of the Sviati Hory national park on the Siverskyi Donets chalk hills were about 80% devastated by 2024, by NGL.media's estimate.
The left-bank terraces of the Siverskyi Donets carry pine forest.
Near Lyman in 2022, Ukrainian forest positions were sandy trenches, with the enemy about 300 m away behind tall pines.
notes: The key-figures table dates this to May 2022.

text: The Serebriansky forest SW of Kreminna mixes forest, swamp and meadow.
The Serebriansky protected reserve covers 107.1 ha within a much larger pine forest.
The Serebriansky forest was contested from autumn 2022 (e3–e8).
notes: End month taken from the full capture in December 2025.

text: Terrikons (terykony) are conical coal-waste heaps that act as artificial high ground.
The Avdiivka terrikon is about 40 m high.
The defenders of the Avdiivka terrikon "saw every Russian move from the heights", and its steep slope stopped assaults.

cites.quote: saw every Russian move from the heights

text: Toretsk has two waste dumps over 100 m high.
Terrikons shaped fire control around Pokrovsk and Selydove.
The Zaporizhzhia steppe is flat to gently rolling, so observation lines are long.
The Siverskyi Donets is 1,053 km long, about 950 km of it in Ukraine.
The Siverskyi Donets has an asymmetric valley and a wet floodplain with willow, birch and alder.
Russian attempts to cross the Siverskyi Donets above Lysychansk failed in May 2022.
Other named front rivers near Pokrovsk include the Vovcha and the Kazennyi Torets.
Large pine massifs line the Oskil as well as the Siverskyi Donets.
To take Kupiansk, Russia had to cross the Oskil, and the pre-war bridge there was destroyed.
Ukrainian aircraft typically strike the floating spans whenever Russian engineers build pontoons across the Oskil at Kupiansk.
Russian troops entered Kupiansk through the disused Shebelynka–Ostrohozhsk gas pipeline, "a walk of about 10 km in darkness" that exits in a forest.

cites.quote: a walk of about 10 km in darkness

text: Ukraine retook about 90% of Kupiansk by December 2025 after disabling the gas-pipeline infiltration route.

text: According to Ukraine's Khartia corps, by September 2026 the Shebelynka–Ostrohozhsk pipeline had become a Russian escape route from Kupiansk.
notes: Source text says only 'an escape route'; that it served Russian troops is implied by context.

text: Pipelines, culverts and utility tunnels are terrain objects in their own right.
The Mokri Yaly river is 147 km long with a 2,660 km² basin.
The Mokri Yaly runs north from the Azov Upland through Velyka Novosilka to the Vovcha.
The Mokri Yaly was a German defensive line in 1943.
In June 2023 Russian forces blew up the hydro facility near Novodarivka on the Mokri Yaly "to slow down our advance", flooding both banks, according to the Ukrainian spokesman Valeriy Shershen.
Small dams on steppe rivers are flood triggers.
In August 2026 Russian groups took eastern Mala Tokmachka and crossed north over the Kinska River, attacking Ukrainian trenches on the tactical heights beyond.

cites.quote: crossed north over the Kinska River

text: The Kinska at Orikhiv shows a recurring terrain pattern: a small river with heights on the far bank.
When the Kakhovka dam was destroyed on 6 June 2023, the Kakhovka reservoir drained.
The Kakhovka reservoir was created by flooding 709,900 ha, including the Velykyi Luh ("Great Meadow") of up to 80,000 ha.

observations.subject: land flooded to create the reservoir

text: Snowmelt in March 2024 partly re-flooded the drained Kakhovka reservoir.
The drained Kakhovka reservoir bed became soft ground that "no equipment, including amphibious vehicles" can cross.
By May 2026 more than 2,000 km² of the old Kakhovka reservoir bed held a young willow-dominated forest.
The old Kakhovka reservoir was 3.6 km wide at Kamianska Sich and 13.5 km at Novovorontsovka.

In the game, the Kakhovka area is a terrain state that changes with era: open water, then mudflat (e5), then wetland and scrub (e6–e7), then willow forest (e8–e9), while the Dnipro stays a hard barrier throughout.
Single-storey private houses with gardens make up districts such as Zabalka in Toretsk.
The Zabalka district of Toretsk sits "in unfavorable terrain" below the waste heaps.
Holiday resorts, children's camps and cottages in the Donbas pine woods served as military positions.
In the game, Donbas pine-wood resorts and cottages can stand in for dacha settlements.

Khrushchevky are Soviet apartment blocks built from 1956 to the mid-1970s, usually 4–5 storeys (no lift required at 5 storeys or fewer), in panel or brick, with basements, including Ukrainian design series.
Toretsk's high-rise centre was demolished by Ukrainian engineers to deny it to Russian troops.

text: The Avdiivka industrial zone (promzona, "promka") near Yasynuvata-2 station was the first line of defence, with reinforced-concrete positions linked by trenches and tunnels, less than 10 km from Donetsk.
The mining towns of Toretsk, Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad and Selydove pair mine shafts and waste heaps with apartment blocks and private-house districts.
In the game, industrial and mining towns are dense, concrete and tunnelled, so they are high-cover, high-defence tiles, and terrikons act as line-of-sight dominators.

For the landscape sample, OSM data was queried through the Overpass API on 2026-09-28 for five 10 × 10 km front-line boxes, covering natural=tree_row, natural=wood/landuse=forest, landuse=farmland, highway=*, landuse=residential, places and buildings (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL).

In the landscape sample, the OSM data was projected to local metres in python/numpy, and belts were defined as tree_row lines plus wood polygons with a mean width under 60 m and a length over 6× the width.

notes: Also: belt length must exceed 6× its width.

In the landscape sample, settlements are Microsoft building footprints (release 2026-02-03) clustered on a 100 m grid.

text: The Huliaipole E sample box is the clean reference grid: OSM and Sentinel-2 agree within 1% on its 550 m main-belt spacing.
In the Huliaipole E sample box the imagery shows cross-belts about 1.1–1.3 km apart, giving belt blocks of about 0.55 × 1.2 km split into 40–50 ha crop fields.
The Robotyne sample box shows the same grid pattern as Huliaipole E rotated about 10°, with main belts about 0.5–0.6 km apart and cross-belts 1.0–1.2 km apart.
In the Kupiansk E sample box the forest-steppe fields are larger and less regular, and wooded balkas cut across them.
In the Chasiv Yar S sample box the ground is dissected, with large woods and fragmented fields.
OSM belt mapping is uneven: west of Pokrovsk almost no belts are mapped, and they exist only as the gaps between farmland polygons, which the imagery shows follow the belts closely.
In the best sample boxes about two-thirds of the shelterbelts visible in Sentinel-2 are mapped in OSM, so OSM belt densities are lower bounds and OSM spacings upper bounds.

text: OSM buildings are 1–18% complete in the sample boxes, so building counts must come from Microsoft footprints, not OSM.
The Sentinel-2 belt detector works only in clean grids; crop stripes, tracks and (south of Chasiv Yar) wartime earthworks cause false detections.
The Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery used for the sample is from 2021 and so shows the pre-invasion landscape.
OSM farmland polygons sometimes split one belt block into several fields, which biases measured field sizes low.
In the spring thaw (March–April), chernozem becomes "liquid earth": mud over still-frozen subsoil that makes fields impassable, while shelterbelts are leafless and give little cover.
During the spring thaw, off-road vehicle movement stops and heavy traffic keeps to paved roads, while infantry and quad bikes keep moving but are slowed.
In late spring (mid-April to May) the ground hardens and foliage expands.
Mechanised assaults resumed near Pokrovsk by mid-April 2025 as the ground hardened.
In late spring, infiltration along treelines rises, and defenders prepare treelines before the leaves come in.
In summer (June–September) the ground is dry and firm and belts have full canopy; dust is likely, but no source on it was retrieved.
notes: Dust is flagged in the file as unsourced.

text: In summer, leaves hide treeline positions from drones and precision fires.
In autumn (October–November), rains bring the autumn rasputitsa and armies shift to the defensive, as in November 2023.
In autumn, leaf-fall exposes treeline positions, so detection rises and mobility falls.
In winter with snow the ground is frozen, as cold as −20 °C in 2026.
notes: The key-figures table dates the −20 °C low to winter 2025–26.

text: In winter with snow, bare dark treelines stand out against white snow.
In winter with snow, tracks in snow lead drones to positions, and movement on snow is readily detected.
In snowy winter conditions, troops wear white ponchos and walk single file.
In winter without snow the ground is frozen or wet and grey; "everything looks grey", and camouflage patterns are harder to match.
In winter and early spring, leafless shelterbelts are more permeable to wind, and blown soil moves mainly in this period.
Fog blinds drones and opens a window for reinforcement and infiltration.
At Avdiivka in November 2023, morning fog gave a window for reinforcement and infiltration.
At Pokrovsk in February and August 2025, fog gave windows for reinforcement and infiltration.
In thick fog on 7–12 November 2025, more than 300 Russian troops got inside Pokrovsk.
At night and in the cold, thermal imaging dominates and is more effective in the cold.
notes: The table row reads 'Thermal imaging, more effective in the cold'.

text: At night and in the cold, troops use thermal ponchos and heated batteries.
Near Kupiansk in December 2024, rain and frost significantly hampered reconnaissance and caused substantial losses of Mavic quadcopters.
Near Kupiansk in December 2024, Russia switched to mechanised assaults to exploit rain and frost that hampered drone reconnaissance.
At Pokrovsk in 2025, wet weather disadvantaged light FPV drones.
Assaults along shelterbelts are timed to rain, fog, darkness and pre-dawn.
In icing and freezing rain, fibre-optic FPVs suffer: ice stops the spool unwinding, and iced fibre snaps or sticks to tree limbs.
In icing conditions, the SFP modules of fibre-optic FPVs, rated for 0–70 °C, lose 20–50%.

text: Under sustained barrages treelines go from intact to thinned to "piles of split wood", and finally to impassable "tangles of fallen timber".
A Sentinel-2 study quantified war damage to protective plantations in front-line hromadas of Kharkiv and Donetsk oblasts.
In front-line hromadas of Kharkiv and Donetsk oblasts, 11.5% of protective forest was damaged by 2022 and 18.1% (145 ± 42 km²) by 2023.
In front-line hromadas of Kharkiv and Donetsk oblasts, 15.8% of shelterbelts were damaged by 2022 and 21.5% by 2023.
In the study area, the area-average loss of cropland-protection function was only 1.9% in 2022 and 2.7% in 2023.
Loss of cropland-protection function reached up to 57% in hotspots near Izium/Balakliia, Vuhledar, Avdiivka and Bakhmut, with Bakhmutska hromada the worst.
Landscapes more than 50 km from battles were "mostly unaffected" in terms of protective plantation damage.
"Low" damage to protective plantations outnumbers "high" damage, and spectral regrowth of herbs hides broken trees, so optical imagery undercounts damage.
Undamaged front-line shelterbelts should be treated as possibly mined.
Between Kharkiv and Luhansk, 24,180 ± 4,715 ha (9.3%) of forest was damaged in April–September 2022, mostly by fires after shelling.
notes: The text gives 'Between Kharkiv and Luhansk'; the key figures call it the Kharkiv–Luhansk AOI.

text: Intense outgoing barrages temporarily defoliated nearby oak woods.

text: A journalistic investigation (NGL.media) counts over 60,000 ha of forest destroyed in Ukraine in two years of war, including Russian logging for fortifications.
The Serebriansky forest was "severely damaged" over three years of fighting.
Marinka had about 9,400 residents before the war.
Marinka went from damaged in May 2022 to "few buildings left standing" by November 2022 and "not a single surviving house" by December 2022.
The battle of Marinka lasted about 20 months.
Toretsk's centre was levelled into "battles among ruins".

OpenStreetMap is a global vector dataset, including Ukraine, with landuse=farmland, natural=tree_row (which explicitly includes shelterbelts), natural=wood/landuse=forest, highways, places and buildings.
OpenStreetMap is licensed under ODbL 1.0, with share-alike on derived databases.
Copernicus DEM GLO-30 is a global digital surface model (including trees and buildings) from 2011–2015 at 30 m (also 90 m), with vertical accuracy better than 4 m LE90.
Copernicus DEM GLO-30 is available under a free licence with attribution to DLR, Airbus and Copernicus.
SRTM GL1 v003 is a radar DEM from February 2000 at 1″ (about 30 m), covering 60°N–56°S.
SRTM GL1 v003 is a US government product available for any use.
ESA WorldCover v200 is a global 11-class land-cover map for 2021 at 10 m (v100 covers 2020).
ESA WorldCover is licensed CC BY 4.0.
Sentinel-2 L2A is global multispectral land imagery from 2017 onward, with a 5-day revisit at 10/20/60 m.
Sentinel-2 data is free and open under the Copernicus Sentinel terms.
Dynamic World V1 gives global per-scene 9-class land-cover probabilities at 10 m from 2015 onward.
Dynamic World is licensed CC BY 4.0.
Hansen GFC v1.12, the dataset behind Global Forest Watch, gives global tree cover in 2000 and annual loss 2001–2024 at about 30 m.
Hansen GFC is licensed CC BY 4.0.
The NASA Harvest Ukraine field-boundary dataset has more than 5 million field polygons of at least 1 ha for 2021–2023, derived from 3 m PlanetScope imagery.

Parish and Müller (2001), Procedural Modeling of Cities, grow road networks with an extended L-system under global goals (pattern templates such as a grid, density maps) and local constraints (water, slope), then subdivide blocks into lots.
The kolkhoz landscape suits the Parish–Müller road model with a strong grid goal: straight belt roads at fixed spacing, snapped to the belt grid.
Vanegas et al. (2012), Procedural Generation of Parcels, subdivide blocks by recursive oriented-bounding-box splitting and straight-skeleton subdivision.
Oriented-bounding-box splitting reproduces rectangular field blocks between belts and narrow house plots along a village street.
Emilien et al. (2012), Procedural generation of villages on arbitrary terrains, is a terrain-aware village growth model covering road seeds, parcels and buildings driven by slope and accessibility.

mentions.name: Procedural generation of villages on arbitrary terrains

text: The Emilien et al. village model fits linear villages following valleys and balkas.
Galin et al. (2010), Procedural Generation of Roads, route roads across terrain by weighted shortest path with slope, water and vegetation costs and bridges.
The Galin et al. road model suits inter-village roads crossing gullies and floodplains.
Smelik et al. (2014), A Survey on Procedural Modelling for Virtual Worlds, maps the field across terrain, vegetation, water, roads and settlements.

mentions.name: A Survey on Procedural Modelling for Virtual Worlds

text: Patel (2010), Polygon Map Generation, builds maps from Voronoi and Lloyd-relaxed polygons with elevation, moisture and rivers.
Patel's polygon map method suits irregular macro features (woods, catchments, balka networks) but less so the rectilinear field grid.
